title.narrative: Reduced Emissions from Deforestation (REDD+) in DRC
Stöd för minskade utsläpp av växthusgaser från avskogning (REDD+) i DRK

description.narrative:
The first phase of the Equateur Integrated REDD Program (PIREDD Equateur), implemented by FAO as a Cooperation Partner and WWF as the main implementing partner, with cofinancing from CAFI and Sweden, was deployed as a comprehensive response to deforestation and rural poverty. By placing local communities at the heart of the approach, the program successfully reconciled ecosystem protection with local economic development in a sustainable manner.
Local governance: The project based its actions on restructuring local governance by establishing over 100 Local Development Committees (LDCs), structured inclusively with a minimum of 40% female representation. In parallel, four Agricultural and Rural Management Councils (CARGs) were formed to involve communities in territorial decision-making. Respect for local populations was demonstrated through the rigorous application of the Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) protocol. This ethical process, systematically translated into local languages, ensured the full support of villagers and Indigenous peoples before each development project.
Land tenure security through community forestry: One of the most measurable impacts of this first phase lies in largescale land tenure security. Thanks to the program's technical support, communities obtained the allocation and security of 28 Community Forest Concessions (CFCLs). These concessions cover a total area of 282,251 hectares of protected forest. To support this management, 14 Simplified Management Plans (PSGs) were finalized by the project and technical partners. This could help legally transfer control of resources to the communities.
Sustainable agriculture and energy: To curb deforestation linked to slash-and-burn agriculture, the project supported more than 690 pilot farmers through Payments for Ecosystem Services (PES) mechanisms. This incentive enabled the establishment of 3,411 hectares of sustainable crops, divided into perennial plantations, improved food crops, and agroforestry plots. In addition, 8,043 hectares of savanna were protected to prevent bushfires. In the energy sector, the fuelwood challenge was addressed through the creation of 909 hectares of plantations dedicated to sustainable charcoal production and the distribution of 6,817 improved cookstoves, drastically reducing household dependence on primary forest areas.
Empowerment: The intervention structured the exploitation of non-timber Forest products (NTFPs), such as leaf harvesting and mat making, into income generating activities derived from the forest. These income generating activities injected tens of thousands of dollars directly into household economies. This economic diversification has offered a concrete and profitable alternative to forest destroying activities, proving that a green development model is possible in the province of Equateur.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
